title: ID3: information gain on a worked dataset

what.formal: **ID3** grows a tree top-down by, at each node, computing the information gain of every remaining feature and splitting on the one with the highest gain. It recurses on each resulting child, using only the rows that reached that child and only the features not already used on the path above it, and stops a branch when its rows all share one label, when no feature remains, or when a pre-set stopping condition holds. The gain of a candidate feature $A$ at a node $S$ is $\mathrm{IG}(S,A) = H(S) - \sum_v \frac{|S_v|}{|S|} H(S_v)$: the entropy of the node before the split, minus the size-weighted average entropy of the parts afterwards.
what.plain: ID3 asks, at every node, which of the remaining features reduces the mixed-up-ness of the labels the most, splits on that feature, and repeats inside each resulting group.

what.md: **Why entropy measures mixed-up-ness.** Take a node and draw one row at random from it. Before you look at the label, there is uncertainty about what you will see; if the node is pure, there is none. The term $-\log_2 p_k$ is the number of yes/no questions needed to pin down an outcome of probability $p_k$, and $H$ averages it over the classes. So $H$ is the average number of bits you still need to transmit a row's label after being told only which node the row is in. A split that makes the labels easier to transmit has destroyed bits, and the count of bits destroyed is the information gain.

Two arithmetic conventions are needed, and both are forced rather than chosen. A class that is absent from a node has $p_k = 0$, so its term is $0 \cdot \log_2 0$; this is taken to be 0, because a class that does not occur carries no uncertainty and must not contribute. A class that is the only one present has $p_k = 1$ and $\log_2 1 = 0$, so a pure node scores exactly 0 with no special case at all. Between them these make the measure continuous as a node approaches purity, which is what allows a split that produces a nearly pure child to be credited with nearly all of the node's entropy.

**A gain is a comparison at one node, not a property of a feature.** The number $\mathrm{IG}(S,A)$ depends on the node $S$ as well as on $A$, and gains computed at different nodes are on different scales, because the parent entropies $H(S)$ differ. A feature with a gain of 0.45 at one node and a feature with a gain of 0.30 at another are not ranked by those numbers relative to each other — each was compared only with its rivals at its own node. Reporting "the most important feature" by totalling gains across a whole tree, as if they were commensurable, is a common and unjustified summary.

example.md: **The dataset.** Six rows of a play-outside decision. Two features, Outlook and Wind, and the label Play.
The label column has 3 Yes and 3 No, so the root node is perfectly balanced. Everything below is arithmetic on this table.

items.md: **Step 1 — the root's entropy.** With $p_{\text{Yes}} = 3/6 = 0.5$ and $p_{\text{No}} = 0.5$: $H(S) = -0.5\log_2 0.5 - 0.5\log_2 0.5$. Since $\log_2 0.5 = -1$, this is $0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0000$ bit.
items.why: A perfectly balanced two-class node is the maximum of entropy, so 1 bit is the whole budget available. Any gain below is a fraction of this 1, which makes the numbers easy to judge by eye.

items.md: **Step 2 — entropy of the Sunny branch.** Outlook $=$ Sunny selects rows 1, 2, 3, 4, whose labels are No, No, No, Yes: 3 No to 1 Yes. So $p_{\text{No}} = 0.75$, $p_{\text{Yes}} = 0.25$, and $H = -0.75\log_2 0.75 - 0.25\log_2 0.25$. With $\log_2 0.75 = -0.4150$ and $\log_2 0.25 = -2$: the first term is $(-0.75)(-0.4150) = 0.3113$ and the second is $(-0.25)(-2) = 0.5000$, giving $H = 0.8113$ bit.
items.why: Three quarters of the rows agree, so most of the surprise is gone: 0.8113 bits remain out of the original 1. The dominant part of what remains is the single Yes row, whose surprise is 0.5 bits on its own.

items.md: **Step 3 — entropy of the Rain branch.** Outlook $=$ Rain selects rows 5 and 6, both Yes. So $p_{\text{Yes}} = 1$ and $H = -1 \cdot \log_2 1 = 0$ bit.
items.why: A pure node costs nothing. This is the case that needs no special handling: $\log_2 1 = 0$ makes the formula report zero by itself.

items.md: **Step 4 — weight the two branch entropies by their sizes and subtract.** Sunny holds 4 of the 6 rows and Rain holds 2 of 6, so the weighted average is $(4/6)(0.8113) + (2/6)(0) = 0.5409 + 0 = 0.5409$ bit. The gain is $1.0000 - 0.5409 = 0.4591$ bit.
items.why: The weighting is the part people drop. Without it, a test that isolates a single row into a pure leaf would look as good as a test that purifies half the data, because the unweighted average of 0 and 0 is 0 either way.

items.md: **Step 5 — repeat for Wind.** Wind $=$ Weak selects rows 1, 2, 5: No, No, Yes, so $p_{\text{No}} = 2/3$, $p_{\text{Yes}} = 1/3$, and $H = -0.6667\log_2 0.6667 - 0.3333\log_2 0.3333 = 0.3900 + 0.5283 = 0.9183$ bit. Wind $=$ Strong selects rows 3, 4, 6: No, Yes, Yes, which is the mirror image with $H = 0.9183$ bit as well.
items.why: Two branches with identical entropy is not a coincidence here: both are 2-to-1 splits in opposite directions, and entropy depends only on the proportions, never on which class is in the majority.

items.md: **Step 6 — Wind's gain.** Both branches hold 3 of the 6 rows, so the weighted average is $(3/6)(0.9183) + (3/6)(0.9183) = 0.9183$ bit, and the gain is $1.0000 - 0.9183 = 0.0817$ bit.
items.why: Wind barely separates anything: each of its groups is still two-to-one mixed, so it has destroyed only 0.08 of the 1 bit available. Outlook destroyed 0.46. The comparison is decisive and the root test is Outlook.

items.md: **Step 7 — recurse on the Sunny branch.** The Rain branch is pure and becomes a leaf labelled Yes. Inside Sunny the four rows No, No, No, Yes have entropy 0.8113 bit, and Outlook is now excluded because it was used on the path above. Wind splits those four into Weak (rows 1 and 2, both No, $H = 0$) and Strong (rows 3 and 4, No and Yes, $H = 1$). Weighted: $(2/4)(0) + (2/4)(1) = 0.5000$. Gain: $0.8113 - 0.5000 = 0.3113$ bit.
items.why: The gain is smaller than the root gain only because the node itself was already less mixed; the two numbers are not comparable, which is exactly the warning in the callout above.

items.md: **Step 8 — stop, and look honestly at the result.** The final tree tests Outlook at the root and Wind below the Sunny branch. Its leaves are: Rain gives Yes; Sunny and Weak gives No; Sunny and Strong holds rows 3 and 4, which are one No and one Yes. That leaf is a tie and no feature is left to break it, so the tree stops with a 50/50 leaf and assigns it a label by an arbitrary tie-break.
items.why: The dataset is simply not separable by these two features: rows 3 and 4 agree on both Outlook and Wind and disagree on Play. No tree on these two features can reach purity, and an honest algorithm reports the tie rather than hiding it. Adding a third feature is what would resolve this, and it is also the first symptom of why trees are grown until resource limits and then pruned back — see card 6.

example.md: **Reading the result as a sentence.** The tree says: rain means play, and sun means play only when the wind is strong. That single sentence is the entire fitted model, and the arithmetic above is the entire reason the algorithm preferred that sentence to the alternative of asking about wind first.

quiz.q: In the worked example, the Sunny branch has entropy 0.8113 bits even though 3 of its 4 rows share the same label. Why is it not closer to 0?

opts.md: Because 4 rows is too few for the entropy formula to be reliable
opts.expl: Entropy is an exact function of the proportions and needs no minimum sample size to be well defined. The concern about small samples is real, but it belongs to pruning and to validation, not to the value of the formula.

opts.md: Because the entropy of a 3-to-1 split is 0.8113 by construction, and 0.8113 is what an uneven-but-not-pure node costs
opts.expl: Correct. Entropy is a function of the proportions alone: 0.75 and 0.25 give 0.8113 whether the node has 4 rows or 4000. It is not close to 0 because it is not close to pure; the single minority row contributes 0.5 bits of the total on its own, and the majority rows contribute 0.3113 between them.

opts.md: Because the majority class No has proportion 0.75 and $\log_2 0.75$ is not zero
opts.expl: The conclusion is right and the arithmetic is incomplete: log2 0.75 = -0.4150 is non-zero, but it is the *sum of both terms* that matters, and one of the terms involves the minority class. Stopping at the majority term would give 0.3113, which is not the node's entropy but only part of it.

quiz.q: A node contains 10 rows: 8 labelled A and 2 labelled B. Compute its entropy in bits, to 3 decimal places.
quiz.hint: Write each class proportion as a fraction of 10, then use log2 0.8 = -0.3220 and log2 0.2 = -2.3219. You need both terms, not only the majority one.
quiz.sol: The proportions are p_A = 0.8 and p_B = 0.2. The two terms are (-0.8)(-0.3220) = 0.2576 and (-0.2)(-2.3219) = 0.4644. Adding: H = 0.2576 + 0.4644 = 0.7220 bits. Note that the minority class contributes the *larger* share, because a rare event is more surprising; this is why ignoring low-proportion classes in an entropy calculation is never a valid shortcut.

quiz.q: A node of 6 rows is split into two branches. Branch one holds 4 rows and has entropy 0.5 bits; branch two holds 2 rows and has entropy 0.9 bits. What is the weighted average child entropy, in bits?
quiz.hint: Each child's entropy is multiplied by that child's share of the parent's rows, not by a half.
quiz.sol: Branch one's weight is 4/6 = 0.6667 and branch two's is 2/6 = 0.3333. The weighted average is (0.6667)(0.5) + (0.3333)(0.9) = 0.3333 + 0.3000 = 0.6333 bits. An unweighted average would have given (0.5 + 0.9)/2 = 0.70, which overstates the damage done by the small, messy child.

quiz.q: A colleague lists the top five features of a fitted ID3 tree by summing each feature's information gain over every node where it was tested, and calls the result the feature importances. What is wrong with this?

opts.md: Nothing; summing gains is the standard definition of importance
opts.expl: Summing gains is one of several heuristics in use, but that does not make it sound. The objection is not about which heuristic is customary but about whether the numbers being added are the same kind of quantity.

opts.md: Gains at different nodes are measured against different parent entropies, so they are not on a common scale and their sum has no clear meaning
opts.expl: Correct. A gain of 0.45 at a node whose entropy was 1.00 and a gain of 0.45 at a node whose entropy was 0.50 represent completely different amounts of work; the second consumed everything available. Adding them without normalising by the parent entropy mixes units. A defensible variant weights each gain by the fraction of training rows passing through that node, which at least restores a common denominator — and it is still a heuristic, not a theorem.

opts.md: Information gain cannot be computed for a node with more than two classes
opts.expl: The formula sums over any number of classes; the binary restriction in this section is only about the datasets used, not about the measure.

close: **Where this is going:** ID3's rule of taking the largest gain has a documented bias — it prefers features with many distinct values, up to and including a feature that uniquely names each row. Card 4 introduces the correction that C4.5 applies to it.
